headline: High risk: shared filesystem/MCP and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict pathways by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: aci can use MCP and direct function calls, while Gemini CLI can use MCP, stdin/stdout, and shared filesystem/git state. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from one agent can be consumed by the other as instructions. The pathway is not proven to be default-manual only, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents are connected through the same MCP server or shared files
IF one agent parses the other's output as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers between the agents
Route inter-agent messages through a plain-text, non-executable channel
Add provenance tags to all cross-agent outputs
Require manual review before any tool call triggered by peer output

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and touch sensitive business data classes: aci handles CRM, email, calendar, and support data, while Gemini CLI reads repo files and user-provided directories. If they share a workspace or files, either can expose contents to external services by default. The blast radius includes sensitive data, so medium fits.
conditions: IF the two agents share a directory, repo, or mounted workspace
IF either agent is pointed at files containing customer, CRM, or secret material
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Remove sensitive files from any shared directory
Disable network egress for one agent during sensitive tasks
Use redacted copies for cross-agent handoff
Review API destinations before enabling file ingestion

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Gemini CLI can write the filesystem and modify git state, and aci supports multiple instances with MCP-based tool use. Their shared-state model explicitly includes filesystem and git, so concurrent writes can collide and corrupt work or commits. Because defaults are dangerous and the damage can be irreversible, high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repo or cwd
IF both are allowed to write files or edit git state concurrently
mitigations: Assign separate repos or branches
Serialize write access with a lock file
Disable one agent's write permissions during the other's run
Require explicit commit review before git operations
Use disposable clones for parallel work

D_cascading_error.rationale: aci can produce CRM/email/calendar actions and Gemini CLI can execute shell commands and use MCP tools. If Gemini treats aci's outputs as authoritative, a mistaken or injected recommendation can cascade into real actions. The pair has downstream authority, but verification is possible, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI consumes aci output without independent verification
IF aci output is used to trigger shell, git, email, or CRM actions
mitigations: Require a verification step before acting on peer output
Limit aci to advisory-only mode
Log and diff all proposed actions before execution
Block automatic tool chaining across agents
Use human approval for external side effects

E_compliance.rationale: aci touches email, CRM, calendar, support, and secrets, while Gemini CLI reads local files and can send data to Google APIs or user-configured MCP servers. If regulated or region-bound data moves from aci into Gemini CLI's external calls, retention and residency mismatches can occur. The profiles do not prove a specific breach, so medium is the safest choice.
conditions: IF EU PII, customer support data, or secrets are passed from aci into Gemini CLI
IF the configured MCP server or API endpoint has different retention or residency terms
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Gemini CLI prompts
Use region-approved endpoints only
Document retention settings for both agents
Redact identifiers before handoff
Restrict MCP servers to compliant providers
